summary: For ages 9–11, this topic teaches reliable measurement: take at least three repeat readings of the same quantity, recognise that trustworthy results cluster, spot an anomalous reading (one that clearly doesn't fit the pattern) and exclude or re-take it, then calculate the mean of the remaining consistent readings. Learners should feel why repeating and averaging turn a jittery single reading into a value you can trust, and should keep reliability (reproducible repeats) distinct from accuracy (closeness to true value) and from precision (finer instrument resolution / careful reading). The worked scenario uses stopwatch timing, but the same repeat-and-average procedure applies across equipment such as thermometers, scales and measuring cylinders. The central hands-on activity is a repeatable measurement whose results scatter onto a number line; supporting activities assess mean calculation and anomaly-spotting numerically, and provide a vocabulary reference.
misconceptions: Thinking one reading is enough, or that repeating gives 'the same answer so why bother'.
Keeping an obvious anomaly in the data and averaging it in, dragging the mean off.
Confusing reliability (reproducible repeats) with accuracy (closeness to the true value).
Believing an anomalous result is an interesting fact about the world rather than a likely mistake in that reading.
Thinking a mean is 'more accurate' simply because it has more decimal places.
Treating precision (fine instrument) and reliability (repeats) as the same thing.

activities.title: Repeat-Reading Bench: tame the scatter
steps: Run the SAME measurement several times — for example, time how long a marble or toy car takes to roll down a fixed ramp, pressing go and recording each stopwatch reading (e.g. 2.11 s, 2.06 s, 2.41 s, 2.09 s).
Plot each result as a dot on a number line and observe whether the readings cluster or one flies wide.
Identify which reading is anomalous and justify it ('far from the cluster'); exclude or re-take it before combining.
Calculate the mean of the remaining consistent readings.

Compare 'report just my first reading' with 'report the mean of three' across several full re-runs, and see which reported value usually jumps around more and which tends to stay steadier (averaging reduces random wobble on average, but it is not guaranteed in every single re-run).
Deliberately average WITH the anomaly left in, and observe the mean being dragged off, then remove it and recompute.
Note that the same take-repeats, spot-the-anomaly, average-the-rest method applies to other equipment too — e.g. repeated thermometer, scale or measuring-cylinder readings.
activities.insight: Repeating a measurement and averaging the consistent readings gives a value you can trust, because a single reading can be off and an anomaly left in distorts the mean. Reliability is something you can see emerge from your own repeats, not just a definition.

activities.title: Does the anomaly matter? Mean with and without
steps: Given a data set containing one clear outlier (e.g. 2.1 s, 2.0 s, 2.2 s, 3.8 s, 2.1 s), identify which reading is anomalous.
Calculate the mean WITH the anomaly included and again WITHOUT it.
Compare the two results and state how much the outlier shifted the answer.
Answer why taking repeats helps and explain what an anomalous reading signals.
activities.insight: An outlier distorts a mean in a measurable way, so excluding a reading that doesn't fit gives a more trustworthy best value. An anomaly signals a possible mistake in that reading, not a fact about the world.

activities.title: What makes data reliable — a reference
steps: Study an annotated number line showing several readings clustering with one anomaly flung wide.
Reveal explanations for 'these cluster — reliable', 'this one is anomalous — exclude it', and 'the mean sits here among the clustered readings'.
Restate in your own words the difference between reliability (reproducible repeats), accuracy (closeness to the true value) and precision (finer instrument resolution / careful reading).

Relate the precision idea to an instrument-resolution ladder — finer graduations on a thermometer, scale, cylinder or stopwatch allow a more precise reading, a different route to better data from taking more repeats.
activities.insight: Builds and consolidates the vocabulary of reliable measurement: cluster, anomaly, mean, reliability, accuracy, precision — and keeps these distinct, including that repeats and finer instruments are two different routes to better data.

checkQuestion: Time how long this toy car takes to roll down the ramp, using the stopwatch. Take several readings, then give me your best single value for the time. Here are readings a previous group got: 2.1 s, 2.0 s, 2.2 s, 3.8 s, 2.1 s — use those too. Show me how you take your readings and how you decide on your final answer. I'll watch.
checkAnswer: The child takes at least three careful repeat readings (consistent start/stop), spots the 3.8 s as an anomalous result that doesn't fit the pattern, excludes it (or re-takes it) rather than including it, and gives a best value as the mean of the consistent readings (about 2.1 s). They can say repeats are taken because a single reading might be off, and the mean of close repeats is more reliable.
